introduction: On this Sunday, Jeremiah contrasts the one who trusts in human strength, like a shrub in the desert, with the one who trusts in the Lord, like a tree planted by the water. In the Gospel, Jesus proclaims the Beatitudes and the woes: blessed are the poor, the hungry, those who weep. Paul affirms that Christ has truly been raised from the dead. Let us put our trust in the Lord.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, blessed are those who trust in the Lord. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be poor in spirit and close to the poor. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the poor, the hungry and those who weep: that they may know God's blessing and receive help from their brothers and sisters. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the rich and comfortable: that they may not be satisfied with their own consolation but share with those in need. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are hated or excluded because of their faith: that they may rejoice in their reward in heaven. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that our roots may go deep into God's word, like a tree planted by the water. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, blessed are those who trust in you. Root us in your word, give us hearts that share with the poor, and bring us to the joy of your Kingdom. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Blessed are you who are poor
reflection.body:
Jeremiah paints two pictures. The first is someone "who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from the LORD." He is like "a bush in the desert," dry and lifeless. The second is the one "who trusts in the LORD." He is like "a tree planted by the waters," whose roots reach the river, so that even in a year of drought "its leaf will be green." The psalm uses the same image for the person who meditates on God's law day and night.

In the Gospel, Jesus comes down to a level place and speaks to a great crowd. Luke's version of the Beatitudes is short and direct: "Blessed are you who are poor, for God's Kingdom is yours. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh." He even calls blessed those who are hated and excluded "for the Son of Man's sake."

Then come four woes that turn the world's values upside down: "But woe to you who are rich! For you have received your consolation." Woe to the satisfied, to those who laugh now, to those of whom everyone speaks well. Jesus is not condemning joy, but warning against a life so comfortable that it no longer needs God or notices others.

Paul gives the reason for this hope. If Christ has not been raised, "your faith is vain." But "now Christ has been raised from the dead." The Beatitudes only make sense if there is a resurrection, if God will truly fill the hungry and wipe away tears.

This week, ask yourself where your roots are. What do you rely on when things get hard? Spend time each day with God's word, and let your trust grow deeper. And look for one person who is poor, hungry or weeping, and bring them a blessing.
